name: David Khan

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the night crew on a loader at a large copper mine. My technical diploma got me started, but spotting a loose rock before anyone drives under it is what earned the crew's trust. I like teaching a new driver to listen to the engine rather than just watch a light. My pay is near the bottom for this job, and replacing my broken gearbox left me with less than a month's bills saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our crew that hype fading doesn't repair a tired loader or improve a low wage. I'd rather see training money spent on safe driving than another office announcement about a miracle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can probably keep loading ore, but a small repair bill already has me checking my bank balance. My loader job feels steady; my rent money still depends on the next pay packet arriving whole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the night crew and use the same inspection routine before starting the loader each shift. I'd put twenty each payday aside again after this month's rent, even if rebuilding my reserve takes ages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not frightened of an AI announcement in this picture. I'm anxious because another car repair would leave me choosing between getting to work and paying rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the car needed fixing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I paid the garage and ate what was already in the cupboard for a week. Missing the bus connection after night shift would have meant missing my next shift, so leaving the car broken was hardly a choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you raise with the union first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The lower-paid skilled workers need a wage review before anyone buys more software. I can teach somebody to load safely, but I cannot teach my landlord to accept half the rent.

I'd rather see **training money** spent on safe driving than another office announcement about a miracle.
think: I can probably keep **loading ore**, but a small repair bill already has me checking my bank balance.
My loader job feels steady; my **rent money** still depends on the next pay packet arriving whole.
do: Keep leading the **night crew** and use the same inspection routine before starting the loader each shift.
Put **twenty each payday** aside again after this month's rent, even if rebuilding my reserve takes ages.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, despite expecting the loader work itself to continue.
S0.quote: My loader job feels steady; my rent money still depends on the next pay packet arriving whole.
fieldNote: His **present anxiety** comes from a depleted reserve and low pay, rather than an expectation that modest software will replace loader operators.
He seeks **collective bargaining** over wages in conversation, while his immediate personal plan remains ordinary work and slowly rebuilding savings.

steps.text: Lead night-shift loading and complete the same pre-start inspection
Set aside twenty each payday after paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd support safer planning software if the mine shows us what changes instead of announcing targets from the office. I'd ask our union representative to get training time into writing before the first new loading schedule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loader still needs a driver, but fewer office staff could mean less help when the loading plan goes wrong. I sometimes use AI to tidy notes; I won't trust route advice until someone tests it beside an experienced driver.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union representative this month for paid practice before any software changes our dispatch instructions. I'd try the new dispatch screen beside a trained operator once the mine has shown the trial is safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm still anxious about another repair eating my rent, and now I'm uneasy about who answers when a screen sends the crew to the wrong place. I still expect the mine to need my hands and eyes, but steady shifts don't fix the empty savings account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a convincing trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Let us run the screen against the old dispatch sheet for several shifts and compare the mistakes. A demonstration in a quiet office would not show what happens when the radio drops out underground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our dispatch clerk catches conflicting instructions before we leave the bay. If software takes over that checking, I want the clerk offered another role rather than quietly disappearing from the rota.

I'd ask our **union representative** to get training time into writing before the first new loading schedule.

do: Ask the **union representative** this month for paid practice before any software changes our dispatch instructions.
Try the **new dispatch screen** beside a trained operator once the mine has shown the trial is safe.
feel: **Anxious about bills**, even while practical loader work still looks secure over the next few years.
S1.quote: I'd ask our union representative to get training time into writing before the first new loading schedule.
fieldNote: He accepts **tested change** rather than adopting first, consistent with occasional AI use and his steady approach.
His **union request** concerns paid preparation and displaced colleagues; he expects loader shifts to remain but keeps his baseline worry about rent.

steps.text: Ask the union for paid dispatch-software practice before rollout
Practise the tested dispatch screen beside a trained operator

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that 2028 planning AI and 2031 robot loaders give us different problems to prepare for. I'd demand a paid training place, because telling low-paid drivers to buy courses is no plan at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect driver numbers to shrink when machines can do the loading around 2031, and that keeps me awake. Two years is short when spare money means the coins left after rent and the car journey to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd join the union's training request now and ask the mine to fund an equipment-maintenance course before 2028. I'd cancel my weekend football subscription this month and keep the money for travel if my loading hours fall after 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm lying awake working out how long I could keep the car if the wage shrank. The three years before robot loaders help a little, but I expect the mine to cut people and I could be among them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why maintenance if robots also arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think maintenance is a permanent hiding place from machines. My diploma gives me a starting point, and learning while still being paid might keep me earning during the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in the first year after thinking AI arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep loading while checking every new job notice and whether the promised course actually starts. If the mine refuses paid learning, I'd take my request back to the union rather than spend rent money on an untested course.

I'd demand a **paid training place**, because telling low-paid drivers to buy courses is no plan at all.
think: I expect **driver numbers** to shrink when machines can do the loading around 2031, and that keeps me awake.
Two years is short when **spare money** means the coins left after rent and the car journey to work.
do: Join the **union's training request** now and ask the mine to fund an equipment-maintenance course before 2028.
Cancel my **weekend football subscription** this month and keep the money for travel if my loading hours fall after 2028.
feel: **Alarmed about lost earnings**, with training possible but no cheap way to fund it alone.
S2.quote: I'd demand a paid training place, because telling low-paid drivers to buy courses is no plan at all.
fieldNote: Expected **robot displacement** drives the alarm, while earlier planning changes matter through management's costs rather than direct replacement of his physical tasks.
His **plausible bridge** depends on paid time because his savings cannot cover unpaid study; he promises himself no permanently safe occupation.

steps.text: Join the union request for paid maintenance training before 2028
Cancel the weekend football subscription and keep the travel money

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives the crew time to learn properly if the mine shares the cost. We should put training dates on the calendar now rather than wait for the planning office to change in 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unlike the fast picture, I could build a small reserve before 2031 without missing rent for a course. Robots around 2034 still threaten my loading job, and a maintenance certificate cannot promise work that isn't advertised nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put thirty each payday into a separate account now, then protect the balance through the first year after 2031. I'd attend a paid maintenance taster once the mine shows a working course and ask about jobs before enrolling further.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm anxious, because the end point still includes losing drivers' jobs. Five years lets me imagine a savings balance and a tested course rather than just another bill arriving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes after 2031 in your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the new planning arrangements with what happens to loading shifts and keep the reserve untouched. The extra three years before robot loaders would be for finishing useful training, not assuming the threat had gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no maintenance work is available locally?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the course provider for actual vacancies before paying for another module. There are few mining employers nearby, so a certificate alone would not persuade me to leave a paying job.

We should put **training dates** on the calendar now rather than wait for the planning office to change in 2031.
think: Unlike the fast picture, I could build a **small reserve** before 2031 without missing rent for a course.
Robots around **2034** still threaten my loading job, and a maintenance certificate cannot promise work that isn't advertised nearby.
do: Put **thirty each payday** into a separate account now, then protect the balance through the first year after 2031.
Attend a **paid maintenance taster** once the mine shows a working course and ask about jobs before enrolling further.
feel: **Anxious** but able to plan, with a longer bridge before loader jobs face robots.
S3.quote: We should put training dates on the calendar now rather than wait for the planning office to change in 2031.
fieldNote: The **longer warning** makes gradual saving credible without removing a realistic threat to his job or pretending that local vacancies will appear.
His willingness to learn remains **conditional on evidence**, with a paid taster and vacancy checks fitting his practical rather than early-adopter approach.

steps.text: Save thirty each payday and protect the balance after 2031
Attend a paid maintenance taster and check actual local vacancies

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell younger crew members that ten years is useful only if we spend some of it preparing. The union should seek regular training places, so the people running loaders can learn before planning changes in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll only be 37 in 2036, so retirement won't rescue me from a job that robots could do around 2039. A decade lets me test another skill while earning, but few local employers still limits where I can use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd book a weekend electrical-maintenance taster after speaking to two former students, while keeping my loading shifts. I'd ask the union learning representative for yearly course reviews and keep attending through the first year after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I can breathe more easily than in the two-year picture, but I still worry about having thirty working years left. I'm not expecting the loader to disappear next month; I'm worried about reaching my thirties with only one way to earn.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask former students before booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want to buy a glossy promise when my savings are still small. Someone who has finished the taster can tell me whether the teaching is useful and fits around shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you be doing during 2037?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still be earning on the loader if the work remained, while comparing my course progress with actual maintenance vacancies. If planning AI had changed the roster, I'd ask the union to protect the agreed study time instead of silently dropping it.

say: I'd tell younger crew members that **ten years** is useful only if we spend some of it preparing.
The union should seek **regular training places**, so the people running loaders can learn before planning changes in 2036.
think: I'll only be **37 in 2036**, so retirement won't rescue me from a job that robots could do around 2039.
A decade lets me test another skill while earning, but **few local employers** still limits where I can use it.
do: Book a **weekend electrical-maintenance taster** after speaking to two former students, while keeping my loading shifts.
Ask the **union learning representative** for yearly course reviews and keep attending through the first year after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about a long career, with more room to test an affordable route away from loading.
S4.quote: I'll only be 37 in 2036, so retirement won't rescue me from a job that robots could do around 2039.
fieldNote: His **young age** keeps a decade from becoming a retirement buffer, even though it makes learning alongside paid shifts more feasible.
His **course checks** and recurring union reviews use the warning period without treating maintenance as immune to later automation.

steps.text: Book a weekend maintenance taster after checking former students’ experiences
Ask the union for yearly course reviews and protected study time

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because losing the office work in 2028 could start a cost squeeze before loaders change around 2031. Paid training with a real job at the end would help, and I'd want our union involved before contracts get signed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whether being good at your job actually earns you time to learn the next one. My loader training took years; my rent can fall behind in a fortnight.

headlineQuote: My loader training took years; my rent can fall behind in a fortnight.
portrait: A **27-year-old crew leader**, he operates a copper-mine loader and enjoys teaching new drivers to notice small warning signs.
His **technical diploma** and strong practical skills have not brought high pay, and a car repair exhausted his small reserve.
He supports **shared training** through the union, but will try unfamiliar equipment only after seeing a safe demonstration himself.
Longer warning makes **paid learning** practical; he still doubts that nearby employers could absorb everyone displaced from the mine.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could squeeze his earnings before he can afford training for work beyond the mine.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid training** linked to actual jobs would let him learn without missing rent or leaving safety questions unanswered.
